TIL that 'billion' means different things in different countries. There are several large-number naming systems for integer powers of ten that use the same words with different meanings.

I find it most helpful in the English language to avoid the word billion entirely, rather repeating thousand or million as necessary to achieve the desired order of magnitude. (This corresponds with the long system but avoids milliard.) This system can become strained in time, but at such a scale it is usually best to use scientific notation and dispense with any description in words; even the number of cells in the body or dollars in the world economy can be expressed without too much difficulty.

Yeah, scientific notation seems like the most direct and straightforward way to communicate orders of magnitude, it seems inefficient to have so many different naming systems for a numerical language, which is arguably the one type of language that anyone should be able to understand regardless of their natural language precisely because it's numbers-based. I'm not great at reading scientific notation now, but I'm sure with some practice I'll get used to it.

It is very rare to encounter any values greater than 1012 to 1014, that is the long billion or short trillion; I cannot recall the last time that I found the word Billiard used in my native German. The only cases that come to mind are in supercomputer data storage as expressed in petabytes, and in the American quad to measure world energy use. This latter example shows that when this threshold is crossed, it is typically better to substitute more appropriate units.

Respecting scientific notation, one can simply remember the exponent as the number of cyphers (0) following the 1: thus one hundred, 100 = 102 has two cyphers; a million, 1.000.000 = 106, has six.
